blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Turning an enquiry question into a hypothesis that data can test, and what makes a hypothesis testable rather than vague.

blocks.heading: Hypothesis and aim
blocks.text: An aim says what the enquiry sets out to find, and a hypothesis is the claim about the answer that the data will confirm or reject. A hypothesis is a statement that can be tested by collecting relevant data, analysing it and drawing a conclusion from the evidence, which is why it is written as a claim and not a question. "Does the river get bigger downstream?" is an aim with no claim to test; "the bedload of the river becomes smaller and rounder downstream" is a hypothesis the stones can confirm or reject.

blocks.heading: What makes it testable
blocks.text: A testable hypothesis names the places, the measure and the expected direction. Places: the Kuiseb river above and below the Naukluft confluence, not just "a river". Measure: pebble long-axis in centimetres, not "size". Direction: smaller and rounder downstream, not "different". With those three fixed, the data collection knows what to measure, the analysis knows what pattern would confirm the claim, and the conclusion has something definite to say, true, false or partly true with figures attached. A vague hypothesis collects data that cannot settle anything, so the sharpest sentence of the enquiry is written first.

blocks.heading: Two hypotheses, one method apart
blocks.text: Take the same street and two hypotheses to see the difference a claim makes. "People visit the town centre more on Saturdays than weekdays" names a comparison, a measure, a direction and a time, so the counts can settle it, Saturday against Wednesday, hour by hour. "The town centre is busier at weekends" names a feeling, no measure of busy, no definition of weekend, no direction to test, so no data collection could confirm or reject it and the enquiry would drift. The discipline is the same for a river: "discharge increases downstream" is measurable, width, depth and speed at four sites; "the river gets bigger" is a sketch of an idea. Write the claim, fix the measure, name the direction, and the fieldwork has a destination.

blocks.heading: Where this connects
blocks.text: The hypotheses of the six enquiries in this topic's tasks run on the methods of the next unit, and the conclusion skills of the last unit close them. The river and beach hypotheses draw on the landforms of topics 2.2 and 2.3, and the town hypotheses on the urban geography of topic 1.6.
